newsitem.title: ITALY: Montedison to continue group streamlining.
newsitem.headline: Montedison to continue group streamlining.

text.p: Italian agri-industrial group Montedison is continuing its policy of streamlining the group, managing director Enrico Bondi told the annual shareholders meeting.

Montedison holding companies, already reduced to 58 at end-1996 from 118 in 1993 and currently numbering 51, will be further reduced to seven by 1998 with considerable cuts in structural costs, Bondi told shareholders.

The group's sell-off programme is also continuing. After divestments already carried out for a total of 2.755 trillion lire, Montedison foresees selling its stake in investment company Societe Centrale d'Investissements by 1998.

During the AGM, a representative of fund manager Prime, one of Montedison's institutional shareholders, criticised Montedison for being "neither a conglomerate nor a real investment holding," and urged the group to get rid of its subholdings European Sugar France (ESF) and Montecatini chemical company.
Bondi said," We want to simplify the structure but it is complicated. For ESF and Montecatini the cost/benefit ratio of their elimination is at the moment not favourable."
"(SCI) has no debts but 300 billion lire of liquidity after selling off various activities and we envisage selling our stake by 1998," Bondi said
Montedison holds 26.04 percent of SCI's total capital and 33.3 percent of voting rights with a book value of 238 billion lire on the 1996 balance sheet.

Bondi, referring to divestments, said talks were going on over Montecatini Tecnologie, but he ruled out selling the 11 percent in energy unit Edison which Montedison held above and beyond its controlling stake.

He noted that Franco-Italian food group Eridania Beghin-Say posted a good increase in operating profit and turnover in the first five months of this year, with great success in eastern European countries in the edible oils sector.
He also said that the Montell polyolefins joint venture with Royal Dutch/Shell had increased net operating profit by 11.5 percent thanks to cost control.

Replying to a shareholder's question, Bondi ruled out the possibility of any Montedison free capital increase, noting that the capital reduction carried out in 1996 to wipe out previous losses had enabled the group to resume paying a dividend after four years.
